pi.name: Lyle Simmons
pi.title: Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Lyle Simmons earned a B.S. from Alma College and a Ph.D. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from Michigan State University. He was a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biology at MIT before joining the University of Michigan in 2008. His laboratory studies how bacteria duplicate and repair their DNA, using Bacillus subtilis as a model organism.

lab_description: The Simmons Lab investigates how bacteria duplicate and repair their DNA, using Bacillus subtilis as a model organism, with an emphasis on mechanisms that are conserved in eukaryotes and humans. Current projects include the biochemistry of RNase H enzymes that remove ribonucleotides and RNA-DNA hybrids from the genome, and the use of mutation accumulation lines with whole-genome resequencing to identify mutagenic signatures linked to antibiotic resistance. The lab also uses transposon-insertion sequencing screens to discover uncharacterized genes required for surviving DNA damage, and SMRT sequencing to map N6-methyladenosine sites that regulate gene expression and virulence in B. subtilis and Streptococcus pyogenes. Approaches span genetics, biochemistry, structural biology, genomics, and single-molecule imaging in collaboration with the Biteen lab.

research_areas.title: Ribonucleotide excision repair and RNA-DNA hybrids
research_areas.summary: Biochemical characterization of RNase H enzymes that remove RNA from RNA-DNA hybrids in bacterial cells, combined with mutation accumulation lines and whole-genome resequencing to identify mutagenic signatures of uncorrected ribonucleotides and their connection to antibiotic resistance.

research_areas.title: Discovery of gene function in DNA damage survival
research_areas.summary: Transposon-insertion mutagenesis followed by deep sequencing identifies uncharacterized genes that contribute to survival of DNA damage, addressing the fact that 46.2% of B. subtilis genes have no demonstrated experimental function.

research_areas.title: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulation of gene expression
research_areas.summary: Pacific Biosciences SMRT sequencing maps m6A methylation sites in B. subtilis and Streptococcus pyogenes genomes, revealing how methylation regulates virulence gene expression and bacterial adherence to human cells through changes in RNA polymerase occupancy.
